summary: Defines mechanisms for SIP user agents behind firewalls and NATs to keep client-initiated connections open so proxies can deliver requests to them. It helps handle networks where the server cannot open a connection to the client.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5626 lets a SIP user agent behind a NAT or firewall receive requests over connections it opened itself. It defines registration, flow tracking, keep-alives and recovery when a connection fails.

questions: how do sip phones work behind nat
what is a sip flow token
subtitle: How SIP user agents keep client-opened flows available for incoming calls through NATs and firewalls.

tldr.problem: A SIP proxy may need to open a connection or send a datagram to a user agent, but NATs, firewalls and TLS certificate constraints can prevent inbound connections.
tldr.mechanism: The user agent opens flows to outbound proxies and registers each one with an instance ID and reg-id. Keep-alives maintain and test the flows; proxies route later requests over the same flows.
tldr.outcome: A user agent can register over multiple flows for reliability and recover a failed flow with backoff. RFC 5626 updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3327.

today: RFC 5626 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009. It updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3327; the batch metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 5626.

sections.title: Why SIP Uses Client-Initiated Connections
sections.content:
Many SIP user agents can open a connection to a registrar or proxy but cannot accept a connection initiated from outside. NATs and firewalls commonly restrict incoming connections. A device may also lack a stable DNS name suitable for a TLS server certificate, even though it can open a TLS connection as a client.

RFC 5626 lets a proxy deliver requests over a network flow that the user agent established. It defines how user agents register those flows, keep them active and detect failures. Multiple simultaneous flows can reduce the effect of a failed connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone may be able to contact its SIP server but not accept a new connection from it. This extension lets the server send requests back over the phone's existing connection.

sections.title: Instance IDs, Registration IDs and Flows
sections.content:
A flow is a transport association identified by both hosts' addresses and ports and by the transport protocol. Each user-agent instance has a persistent instance-id, carried in the +sip.instance Contact parameter. The identifier must stay the same across power cycles and network changes.

Each registration over a different flow has its own reg-id. The registrar uses the instance ID to associate registrations with one device and the reg-id to distinguish its flows. A user agent's outbound-proxy-set contains the proxy URIs it will try to keep reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: The instance ID identifies the user-agent device across restarts. A separate reg-id identifies each flow that the device registers.

sections.title: Registering Flows with Proxies
sections.content:
A user agent must support an outbound-proxy-set containing at least two URIs and should support up to four. If the set contains more than one URI, it must register through at least two proxies. Each registration includes the outbound and path option tags in Supported, a persistent instance ID and a reg-id distinct from the other flows for that instance and address of record.

A successful response that requires the outbound option indicates that the registrar and any required edge proxy support the mechanism. An edge proxy that is the first hop places a flow token in a Path header and adds the ob URI parameter. The token identifies the flow and lets the proxy recover it when a later request arrives.

The registrar stores the contact, instance ID, reg-id, Path values and the flow information. An authoritative proxy sends incoming requests over one registered flow. It must not target multiple contacts for the same instance at once; after a 430 Flow Failed response, it should try a different reg-id for that instance.
sections.plainLanguage: The device registers each connection it opens, and the registrar records which device and flow it represents. A flow token lets an edge proxy direct later requests back through the correct connection.

sections.title: Keep-Alives for TCP and UDP
sections.content:
Keep-alives refresh NAT or firewall state and help the user agent detect a failed flow. For connection-oriented transports such as TCP or SCTP, the user agent sends a double CRLF ping and waits for a single CRLF pong. If no pong arrives within 10 seconds, the user agent must treat the flow as failed.

For UDP, the user agent sends STUN Binding Requests over the same flow as SIP. The response must include XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS. A STUN error, no response after seven retransmissions, or a changed mapped address means the flow has failed. Without a Flow-Timer header, the recommended random interval is 24 to 29 seconds for STUN.

If the registration response contains Flow-Timer, the user agent must send keep-alives at least that often. The recommended interval varies randomly between 80% and 100% of the timer value.
sections.plainLanguage: The user agent periodically checks that its connection still works. TCP uses CRLF messages; UDP uses STUN messages, which can also reveal a changed network address.

sections.title: Recovering a Failed Flow
sections.content:
When a registered flow fails, the user agent opens a replacement flow and registers it using the same reg-id as the failed registration. It waits before retrying after a failed attempt so that many devices do not reconnect at once after a server failure.

The upper-bound wait is the smaller of a configured maximum and the base time multiplied by two to the number of consecutive failures. The default maximum is 1800 seconds; the default base time is 30 seconds if every flow has failed and 90 seconds if another flow remains usable. The actual delay is random between 50% and 100% of that upper bound.
sections.plainLanguage: After a flow fails, the user agent waits before trying again. Repeated failures increase the wait, and random delays spread retries across time.

sections.title: How Edge Proxies Protect Flow Tokens
sections.content:
An edge proxy needs a token that uniquely identifies a flow, allows the proxy to recover the flow and cannot be changed by an attacker. The RFC gives a stateless example: combine transport and both endpoints' addresses and ports, then authenticate the value with HMAC-SHA1-80 using a secret key held by the proxy.

When a request returns with a token, the proxy checks its integrity and finds the flow. If the token has been modified, the proxy should return 403 Forbidden. If the flow no longer exists, it should return 430 Flow Failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy uses a protected token to identify the registered flow. It rejects a modified token and reports when the flow it names no longer exists.

sections.title: Keeping Calls Bound to Authenticated Users
sections.content:
The main security goal is to prevent an attacker from redirecting a valid user's calls. The mechanism relies on SIP registration authentication: the registrar stores flow information only after registration succeeds. An instance ID alone is not enough, because an attacker could copy another user's ID.

With edge proxies, the registrar stores a Path value only after successful authentication and later returns it to route requests. An edge proxy routes over a flow only when the request contains a flow token that the proxy created. The RFC does not change SIP's required security mechanisms; it relies on existing Digest authentication and TLS support.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrar accepts a flow only as part of an authenticated registration. This prevents someone from using a copied device identifier to redirect another user's calls.

sections.title: Transport Choices Affect Large Messages
sections.content:
The RFC notes that SIP deployments choose which transports to use. When a UDP request is too large, SIP attempts to switch to TCP. With outbound flows, that switch works only if the user agent has established a suitable TCP flow as well.

A deployment using only UDP outbound flows will fail for sufficiently large SIP messages. The RFC notes that TCP connections require proxies to maintain many active connections, which can affect deployment decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: A UDP-only setup cannot carry every large SIP request. If a request needs TCP, the user agent must already have a TCP flow for the server to use.
